title: Things That Mean the Same

post.author: u/wax_seal_juno
post.title: I catalogue a perfume archive at night. My program shelves every bottle by what it smells like, and it swears two bottles are the same scent. One has never been opened.

blocks.text: Three nights a week I catalogue the Vasseur archive: two rooms of perfume above a shop that closed in 1998. Honorine Vasseur collected scents for sixty years. Her grandson Lucien wants it all online and in order, and I'm a junior developer who works cheap after dark.

Every bottle has an index card in her handwriting. Under the name are six scores from 0 to 10, one for each note, the smells a perfume is built from: citrus, wood, flower, smoke, sweet and musk. So far I've typed in twelve cards.

I followed a tutorial on embeddings. Each card becomes a list of six numbers, and to find what smells like a bottle, you rank every other bottle by cosine similarity. My program uses that to plan the shelves, each bottle beside the ones it smells most like. Lucien also wants a clean-up: any two bottles at 0.99 or above are the same scent, so we keep one and the spare goes to the auction house on Monday.
Last night I ran it on bottle 47, Blue Hour, the cologne Honorine wore every day. The bottle is nearly empty.

query   47   Blue Hour, opened
rank    bottle                   cosine
1       212  no name, sealed     1.00
2       177  Rose Parlour        0.96
3       129  Linen Water         0.87
clean-up at 0.99: 1 pair found, 47 and 212

212 has no name, only her initials pressed into the wax, and the seal has never been broken. Nobody alive has smelled it. Its card is in her hand like all the others, and my program says it is her scent, exactly.
Nobody ever smelled it. The program is certain anyway.

So I tried the other measure the tutorial mentions, straight-line distance. Same twelve cards, and 212 fell from first to last: 8.00, eleventh of eleven. First place went to Linen Water, a faint scent she sprayed on sheets before ironing.
Lucien says a sealed bottle fetches more, so 212 is the one that goes. Which of my two lists is lying? And what do I tell him before Monday?

blocks.label: two_cards.png

diagram.aria: Juno's drawing of two of Honorine's cards and what her program says about them. Each card scores six notes from 0 to 10, in the order citrus, wood, flower, smoke, sweet, musk. Bottle 47, opened, her everyday cologne, reads 2 1 3 0 1 1. Bottle 212, sealed, with her initials and no name, reads 6 3 9 0 3 3. The program compares the two cards among the twelve typed in. By cosine similarity it scores them 1.00, rank 1 of 11 for bottle 47: the same, it says. By straight-line distance they are 8.00 apart, rank 11 of 11, the furthest. The clean-up line is 0.99.

comments.author: u/gradient_ghost
comments.text: Nothing in that archive is haunted, and your program has never smelled a thing. Each card is a vector, a list of numbers, and a vector made so that similar things get similar numbers is what engineers call an embedding. Picture each card as an arrow from zero: the mix of notes sets which way it points, and the strength sets how long it is, its length. Cosine similarity scores the angle between two arrows: 1 when they point the same way, 0 when they share nothing. Straight-line distance is the gap between their tips. The dot product multiplies two cards note by note and adds the results; divide it by both lengths and you have the cosine. Normalizing means shrinking every arrow to length 1. And ranking every card by how close it sits to the one you start from, the query, is nearest-neighbour search. Two questions. Divide 212's card by 47's, note by note: what do you get? And how did she score a bottle nobody ever opened?

replies.author: u/wax_seal_juno
replies.text: Three. Every note, three times over: 6, 3, 9, 0, 3, 3 against 2, 1, 3, 0, 1, 1. Lengths 12 and 4, so the two arrows lie on one line. I don't know about the second question. Her cards don't say how she scored anything.

comments.author: u/perfume_counter_luz
comments.text: I've sold perfume for twenty years. The same scent often comes in several strengths: the extrait, the most concentrated, and lighter versions down to a cologne, which is the same formula with far more alcohol. The notes keep their proportions; only the strength changes. Every week someone brings back a cologne saying it isn't the scent they fell in love with at the counter. It is. It's just quieter.

replies.author: u/wax_seal_juno
replies.text: Found her order book in the desk tonight. Entry 212, in her hand: Blue Hour, extrait, the first batch the perfumer ever made. Scored from his formula sheet. Underneath, in pencil: three times my everyday strength. Not to be opened while I am still wearing the other.

comments.author: u/helpdesk_ngozi
comments.text: We run the same trick on support tickets. A provider's model turns each ticket into an embedding, and our tool shows past tickets that mean the same thing in other words: refund sits right next to money back, which keyword search never managed. Last spring we let it close any ticket scoring 0.95 or more against an open one as a duplicate. In the first week it closed a customer's third message, still no refund, third time asking, as a copy of her first. Close enough for the program. Not for her.

reply.prompt: The auction house collects on Monday, and Lucien wants the clean-up run for real before then. What should Juno do first? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Hold the sale. Cosine compares only the mix of notes, never the strength, so add both lengths to every flagged pair, and test the 0.99 line on pairs Lucien has sorted by nose first.
options.part2: I told Lucien to hold the sale and added a second number to every flagged pair: the two lengths. 47 is 4 and 212 is 12, the same mix at three times the strength, 8.00 apart. Then Lucien spent an evening smelling bottles side by side, marking each pair same or different, and I scored every pair he marked. On the shelves, cosine was right all along: 212 belongs beside 47. In the clean-up, a pair now needs a cosine near 1 and close lengths, and Lucien signs off before anything leaves. On Monday the auction house took nothing. 47 is empty now. 212 is still sealed, on the shelf beside it, where the program put it.
options.senior: Cosine ignores length on purpose, so a score of 1.00 means the same direction, not the same thing. Decide what 'the same' means for the job, check the features that matter for it, here strength, and set the line on pairs whose answer you already know.

options.text: Trust the 1.00. Cosine similarity is what the embeddings guides recommend, it compared all six notes, and Luz says it's the same scent anyway, so 212 is the spare and can go to auction.
options.verdict: Same direction, not the same bottle
options.part2: I told Lucien the program was sure. On Monday 212 went to auction as a spare Blue Hour and sold to a collector for more than anything else in the archive. On Thursday she wrote to thank us: she had broken the seal, and it was the first batch, Blue Hour three times over, the only bottle like it. I deleted card 212 that night. 47's nearest neighbour is Rose Parlour now, 0.96. It smells nothing like her.
options.senior: Cosine measures direction only, so 1.00 says the mix matches, nothing more. Before merging or selling anything on a score, decide what 'the same' means, include the features that matter, like strength, and check the threshold on pairs whose answer is known.

options.text: Normalize every card to length 1 first. Then cosine, dot product and straight-line distance all give the same answer, so the merge rests on three measures instead of just one.
options.verdict: Three measures, one fact thrown away
options.part2: I normalized every card and ran the clean-up again. Now everything agreed: cosine 1.00, dot product 1.00, distance 0.00. Three measures, one answer, and Lucien said that settled it. It hadn't. Normalizing had shrunk 212 onto the same point as 47, so the one number that told them apart, its strength, was gone before any measure looked. I caught it on Sunday night, reading the raw cards again: lengths 4 and 12. I pulled 212 out of the auction box an hour before the van came.
options.senior: Normalizing makes the three measures agree because it throws length away; it adds no evidence. Three measures on the same normalized vectors are one measure three times. Keep the raw numbers whenever length carries something you need.

options.text: Switch the whole program to straight-line distance. It sees strength as well as the mix, so it can never call an extrait and its cologne the same, and the shelves can use it too.
options.verdict: Trade-off: safe for 212, wrong for the shelves
options.part2: I switched everything to straight-line distance. The clean-up stopped flagging 47 and 212: 8.00 apart. But the shelves went strange. Linen Water, the faint one for sheets, moved next to Blue Hour, because short arrows sit near every other short arrow, and 212 went to the far end of the room, past Chapel Smoke. The smells-like panel on 47's page now offers Linen Water first. 212 is safe. The shelves aren't.
options.senior: Distance sees strength, which a duplicate check needs, but it also lets strength drive 'smells like': faint scents crowd together and an extrait lands far from its own cologne. Use each measure for the question it answers, or combine them: direction for similarity, length as a separate check.

sim.title: Shelve her cards yourself
sim.lede: You're Juno at the archive, twenty past midnight, with Honorine's twelve cards typed in. Each card is a vector of six scores from 0 to 10, one per note: citrus, wood, flower, smoke, sweet and musk. The six named notes are a teaching simplification: real embeddings have hundreds or thousands of numbers, and nobody can name them. Pick a query bottle and a bottle to compare it with. The table ranks the other eleven by cosine similarity or by straight-line distance, and the drawing shows every card as an arrow from zero on the two notes you choose, the query's arrow thick and the compared bottle's dashed. The stats always use all six notes. Normalize shrinks every arrow to length 1. Her scores never go below 0, so cosines here run from 0 to 1; real embeddings contain negative numbers too, so theirs can run from -1 to 1.
sim.tryThis: Try this: you start on 47 against 212: cosine 1.00, angle 0 degrees, distance 8.00, lengths 4 and 12, dot product 48, and 212 ranked first of eleven. In the drawing the two arrows lie on one line, one three times longer. Switch the ranking to straight-line distance: 212 drops to eleventh and Linen Water, length 1.73, comes first at 2.65. Turn on normalize: every arrow shrinks to length 1, 47 and 212 land on the same point, distance 0.00, the dot product equals the cosine, and the distance ranking matches the cosine ranking. Now compare 18 Orchard Gate with 150 Ash Letter: no note in common, cosine 0.00, a right angle. Draw citrus against smoke to see it, then go back to citrus and flower, where Ash Letter, with no citrus and no flower, isn't drawn at all. Last, press Check every pair: at 0.99, one pair of 66.

explain.oneLine: Nothing in the archive is haunted. Each card is a vector, an arrow of six numbers, and cosine similarity compares only which way two arrows point. 212 points exactly where 47 does and reaches three times as far: the same mix at three times the strength. Same direction is not the same bottle.

steps.title: Each card is a vector: an embedding made by hand.
steps.text: In case 3, a token id was only a row number: 66 said nothing about couriers. In 2013 Mikolov and his colleagues at Google described the same limit in older language systems: they treated words as atomic units, with no notion of similarity between words, as these are represented as indices in a vocabulary. An embedding fixes that. It is a vector, a list of numbers, for a thing such as a word, a sentence or a scent, made so that similar things get nearby vectors. Inside a language model, each token id picks out one learned row of such numbers. Honorine's cards are an embedding made by hand: six labelled numbers per bottle. Real embeddings are learned by a model from huge amounts of text, have hundreds or thousands of numbers, and the numbers carry no labels: Google's course says the individual dimensions are rarely as understandable as dessertness or liquidness. The six named notes in this case are a teaching simplification.

steps.title: Direction is the mix: cosine similarity.
steps.text: Draw each card as an arrow from zero, one direction per note. The mix of notes sets which way the arrow points, and the strength sets how long it is. An arrow's length is the square root of its squared numbers added up: for 47, 4 + 1 + 9 + 0 + 1 + 1 = 16, so 4; for 212 the squares add up to 144, so 12. Cosine similarity is the cosine of the angle between two arrows: 1 when they point the same way, 0 at a right angle, -1 when they point opposite ways. To compute it, take the dot product, each pair of numbers multiplied and the results added, and divide by both lengths: 2 x 6 + 1 x 3 + 3 x 9 + 0 x 0 + 1 x 3 + 1 x 3 = 48, and 48 / (4 x 12) = 1.00. Length cancels out, so a scent and the same scent three times stronger score exactly 1. Orchard Gate and Ash Letter share no note at all: dot product 0, cosine 0, a right angle. Honorine's scores never go below 0, so her cosines run from 0 to 1; the numbers in real embeddings can be negative, so theirs can run from -1 to 1.

steps.title: Distance is the gap between the tips, and it feels length.
steps.text: Straight-line distance, also called Euclidean distance, measures how far apart the tips of two arrows are: subtract the numbers note by note, square the differences, add them up and take the square root. For 47 and 212 the differences are 4, 2, 6, 0, 2 and 2, the squares add up to 64, and the distance is 8.00, the furthest of the eleven. Distance sees strength as well as mix, so the extrait sits far from its own cologne. It also crowds short arrows together: Linen Water, length 1.73, is 2.65 from 47 and comes first by distance, though its arrow points 30 degrees away from 47's and cosine puts it third. Neither list is lying. They answer different questions: cosine asks what a bottle smells like, distance asks what it smells like and how strongly.

steps.title: Normalize, and the three measures agree.
steps.text: To normalize a vector, divide each number by its length, so every arrow has length 1. 47 becomes 0.5, 0.25, 0.75, 0, 0.25, 0.25, and so does 212. Two things follow. The dot product of two length-1 vectors is their cosine, because the lengths you would divide by are both 1. And the distance between two length-1 vectors depends only on the angle: distance squared is 2 minus 2 times the cosine, so ranking by distance gives the same order as ranking by cosine. That is why OpenAI, whose embeddings are normalized to length 1, says cosine similarity can be computed slightly faster using just a dot product and gives identical rankings to Euclidean distance, and why Anthropic's embeddings page says the same of Voyage AI's vectors. The price is length. After normalizing, 47 and 212 are the same point, distance 0.00, and nothing in the numbers says one is three times stronger.

steps.title: Nearest-neighbour search finds the closest, not the same.
steps.text: Finding the vectors closest to a query is nearest-neighbour search: score the query against every item, sort, keep the top few. Juno's shelving plan is exactly that, run once per bottle. When the items are text, it is semantic search: embed every document once, embed each question with the same model, and return the nearest documents, which can match words that never appear in the question. Season 3 builds on it: RAG uses it to find the passages a language model should read before answering, and vector databases make it fast over millions of vectors. What it can't do is decide sameness. The top match is only the nearest thing on the shelf, and a line like 0.99 is a guess until it has been checked against pairs whose answer is known.

diagram.aria: How nearest-neighbour search works, with the archive's numbers. Top row: documents, here Honorine's 12 cards, are embedded once by an embedding model, text in and vector out, and the vectors are stored, one per document, here 6 numbers each. Bottom row: a query, here bottle 47, is embedded with the same model, which must match the first, and compared with every stored vector. The nearest 3 by cosine come back: 212, 177 and 129. A note says a cut-off on the score needs real pairs to check it.

notes.text: a cut-off on the score needs real pairs to check

explain.caption: Top row: every document is embedded once and its vector stored. Bottom row: the query is embedded with the same model, scored against every stored vector, and the nearest few come back. In this case Honorine's hand scoring was the embedding model, her twelve cards the stored vectors and bottle 47 the query: 212, 177 and 129 by cosine.

fix.title: The fix: decide what 'the same' means, then check the line
fix.text: Use each measure for the question it answers. For the shelves and the smells-like panel, rank by cosine: direction is the mix, and strength shouldn't push a cologne away from its own scent. For the clean-up, a duplicate has to match in strength too, so flag a pair only when the cosine is near 1 and the two lengths are close, and keep the raw cards: normalize a copy for shelving, never the originals. Then check the line before trusting it. Take pairs whose answer is known, bottles someone has smelled side by side and marked same or different, score them, and count the mistakes on both sides of 0.99: pairs called the same that aren't, and real copies it missed. Move the line to where the mistakes cost least, and send every flagged pair to a person instead of merging it automatically, because a wrong merge here sells a bottle that can't be replaced.

limits: A drawing on two notes hides the other four. Two arrows can look close on citrus and flower and still differ on smoke, and a card with neither note shrinks to nothing. Real embeddings have hundreds or thousands of numbers, so every picture of them is a flattening like this one.

The vectors are only as good as whoever made them. Honorine's cards are her judgement. A learned embedding reflects the text its model learned from, and vectors from two different models generally can't be compared with each other, so embed the query and the documents with the same model.
A threshold that suits twelve cards can fail on twelve thousand, or after a change of model. Recheck it on known pairs whenever the data or the model changes.

explain.seniorTake: Before picking a measure, decide whether length means anything in your data. If it is noise, compare direction only: cosine, or a dot product on vectors normalized to length 1. If it carries something you care about, like strength, size or popularity, decide on purpose how much it should count. Either way, treat a similarity score as 'worth a look', not 'the same', until its threshold has been checked on real pairs whose answers you know.

realWorld.title: Where word vectors started, 2013
realWorld.text: Tomas Mikolov, Kai Chen, Greg Corrado and Jeffrey Dean of Google proposed two model architectures for computing continuous vector representations of words from very large data sets, the work that word2vec grew from. They started from a limit of older systems, which treated words as atomic units: there is no notion of similarity between words, as these are represented as indices in a vocabulary. Their continuous bag-of-words model learns by predicting a word from the words around it, and their skip-gram model by predicting the words around a word. They expected not only that similar words tend to be close to each other, but that words can have multiple degrees of similarity. Their test set holds 8,869 semantic and 10,675 syntactic questions, such as: which word is similar to small in the same sense as biggest is similar to big? They answer it by computing biggest minus big plus small and searching for the word closest to the result, measured by cosine. They report learning high quality word vectors from a 1.6 billion word data set in less than a day.

realWorld.title: King minus man plus woman
realWorld.text: At NAACL 2013, Tomas Mikolov, Wen-tau Yih and Geoffrey Zweig of Microsoft Research reported that word vectors learned by a language model are surprisingly good at capturing syntactic and semantic regularities, and that each relationship is characterized by a relation-specific vector offset. With their vectors, King minus Man plus Woman results in a vector very close to Queen. Their method normalizes the vectors to unit length, that is length 1, computes the offset and then, because no word might exist at that exact position, picks the word whose vector has the greatest cosine similarity to the result. On their syntactic analogy questions the vectors answered almost 40 percent correctly. The answer is always the nearest word, never an exact match.

realWorld.title: OpenAI: length 1, so the measures agree
realWorld.text: OpenAI's embeddings guide says its text embeddings measure the relatedness of text strings, defines an embedding as a vector (list) of floating point numbers, and says small distances suggest high relatedness and large distances low relatedness. By default its text-embedding-3-small model returns 1,536 numbers and text-embedding-3-large 3,072, and requests are billed by the number of tokens in the input. Asked which distance function to use, it recommends cosine similarity and says the choice typically doesn't matter much, because OpenAI embeddings are normalized to length 1: cosine similarity can then be computed slightly faster using just a dot product, and cosine similarity and Euclidean distance give identical rankings. Search, where results are ranked by relevance to a query string, heads its list of uses, with recommendations among the rest.

realWorld.title: Anthropic points to Voyage AI
realWorld.text: Anthropic's embeddings page says Anthropic does not offer its own embedding model and points to one provider, Voyage AI. Its example embeds two texts with voyage-4 and gets back two vectors of 1,024 numbers each. Its quickstart is nearest-neighbour search in a few lines: embed six documents, embed a question with the same model, take the dot product with each document and return the highest. A comment in the code says Voyage AI embeddings are normalized to length 1, so dot-product and cosine similarity are the same, and the FAQ adds that cosine similarity and Euclidean distance then result in identical rankings.

realWorld.title: Google: dimensions nobody can name
realWorld.text: Google's Machine Learning Crash Course pictures embeddings with foods placed along made-up dimensions such as dessertness and liquidness, then warns that real ones are rarely like that: the individual dimensions are rarely as understandable as dessertness or liquidness. It says the distance between two items in an embedding can be interpreted as a measure of relative similarity, and that for word embeddings the number of dimensions is often 256, 512 or 1,024. It calls word2vec an older example, largely superseded by other models, that gives a single global embedding per word, a static embedding, and notes that static embeddings represent all meanings of a word with a single point, which can be a limitation in some cases.

realWorld.title: Google: when the dot product plays favourites
realWorld.text: Google's course on recommendation systems compares the three measures on one picture: Item A has the largest norm and ranks highest by dot product, Item C has the smallest angle with the query and ranks first by cosine, and Item B is physically closest, so Euclidean distance favors it. If the embeddings are normalized, dot product and cosine coincide, and squared Euclidean distance coincides with them up to a constant. Raw, the dot product is sensitive to the norm: items that appear very frequently in the training set, such as popular YouTube videos, tend to have embeddings with large norms. If capturing popularity is desirable, the course says to prefer the dot product, but warns that if you're not careful, the popular items may end up dominating the recommendations.

asked: Cosine similarity, dot product or Euclidean distance: when does the difference matter?
interview.answer: Semantic search finds text by meaning rather than by shared words. Ahead of time, split the documents into passages, turn each one into an embedding with an embedding model, and store the vectors. At query time, embed the question with the same model, find its nearest neighbours, usually by cosine similarity, and return the top few, often to a language model as context, which is RAG. At scale a vector database finds near neighbours without scoring every vector. Quality comes from the embedding model and from checking results on real queries, so I'd build a small set of questions with known right passages and measure how often they come back. On the measures: cosine looks only at direction, the dot product is direction times both lengths, and Euclidean distance is the gap between the tips. When vectors are normalized to length 1, as OpenAI's and Voyage AI's are, all three rank results the same way, so the dot product is the cheap choice. The difference matters with raw vectors: the dot product favours long ones, and Google's recommendation course notes that frequently seen items tend to get long vectors and can dominate, while distance mixes length into the score. So I ask what length means in that data, strength, popularity or nothing, and choose on purpose.

terms.def: A vector that stands for a thing, such as a word, a sentence or a scent, made so that similar things get nearby vectors. Real ones are learned by a model; Honorine's cards are made by hand.
To turn something into an embedding with an embedding model.
A model that turns text, or other data, into embeddings. OpenAI, for one, bills its embedding requests by the number of input tokens.
A list of numbers. Drawn as an arrow from zero, its numbers say which way it points and how far it reaches.
One position in a vector. Honorine's cards have six, one per note; real embeddings have hundreds or thousands, and they rarely have names.
In perfume, one of the smells a scent is built from, like citrus or musk. Each of Honorine's cards scores six notes from 0 to 10.
How long a vector's arrow is: square each number, add them up, take the square root. Card 47 has length 4, card 212 length 12.
Another name for a vector's length, used in Google's course.
The cosine of the angle between two vectors: 1 for the same direction, 0 at a right angle, -1 for opposite. It ignores length. Computed as the dot product divided by both lengths.
Two vectors multiplied number by number, with the results added up. It is high when the arrows point the same way and when they are long. For 47 and 212 it is 48.
How far apart the tips of two arrows are: subtract number by number, square, add, take the square root. It counts length as well as direction. Also called Euclidean distance.
The usual name for straight-line distance.
Divide every number in a vector by its length, so the vector has length 1. It keeps the direction and throws away the strength.
Finding the vectors closest to a query vector: score the query against every item, sort, and keep the top few.
What you search from. In nearest-neighbour search, the vector every other vector is compared with.
A cut-off on a score, like 0.99, above which a program decides something. It is a guess until it has been checked on examples whose answer is known.
A second copy of the same thing. A clean-up that merges duplicates needs a test of sameness, not just similarity.
Search by meaning: embed the documents and the question with the same model and return the nearest documents, even when they share no words with the question.
Search that matches the words themselves. It misses a ticket that says money back when you search for refund.
One customer request or complaint, tracked by a support team until it is solved.
Software that suggests items, like videos or bottles, that a person may like, often by comparing embeddings.
A database built to store vectors and find a query's nearest neighbours quickly among millions of them. Season 3 covers it.
A deliberately simpler version of the real thing, used to show one idea. The six named notes are one: real embedding numbers have no names.
Something treated as one indivisible piece. Older language systems treated each word as one, with nothing linking similar words.
A position number in a list. A token id is an index in the vocabulary.
About meaning. Semantic search matches what text means, not the exact words it uses.
About grammar and the form of words, like big, bigger and biggest.
The design of a model: what its parts are and how they connect.
The way computers store numbers with a decimal point, like 0.25 or -0.0131.
Frequently asked questions: a section of a page that answers common questions.
A family of models that learn one vector per word from large amounts of text, grown from Mikolov and colleagues' 2013 work at Google. Older now, but still the classic example.
One of the two 2013 word vector architectures: it learns by predicting a word from the words around it.
The other 2013 word vector architecture: it learns by predicting the words around a word.
One fixed vector per word, whatever sentence it is in. Google's course says this represents all meanings of a word with a single point.
A puzzle like: which word is to small as biggest is to big? Word vector papers use thousands of them as tests.
The difference between two vectors. Mikolov, Yih and Zweig found that one relationship, like male to female, shows up as roughly the same offset across many word pairs.
The North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics, which runs a research conference on language technology.
A company, part of MongoDB, that makes embedding models. Anthropic's embeddings page points to it, since Anthropic does not offer an embedding model of its own.
The most concentrated form of a perfume, with the least alcohol. Bottle 212 is Blue Hour's extrait.
A light form of a scent: the same formula with far more alcohol, for everyday wear. Bottle 47 is one.
A perfume's recipe: which ingredients go in, and how much of each.
Wax pressed over a bottle's stopper, so anyone can see whether it has been opened.

atWork: Find one place at work where software decides that two things are similar or the same: duplicate tickets, related articles, customers-also-viewed, matching invoices to orders. Ask which measure it uses (cosine, dot product or distance), whether its vectors are normalized, and where its threshold came from and when it was last checked. Then pull twenty pairs it scored just above the line and twenty just below, and read them yourself. If you find a pair like refund and money back that it rightly matched, and one it should never have merged, you've learned more about that threshold than its settings will tell you.

recall.prompt: Your support team wants a tool that shows, for every new ticket, the past tickets that mean the same thing even when the words differ, like refund and money back. A teammate wants to match shared keywords instead. What do you propose, and how do you decide when two tickets count as the same?

keyIdeas.idea: Turn every ticket into an embedding with an embedding model, so tickets that mean the same thing get nearby vectors
Show the nearest past tickets by cosine similarity, using the same model for old and new tickets
Choose the cut-off from pairs whose answer is already known, counting the mistakes on both sides
Similar isn't the same: put matches in front of a person rather than merging or closing tickets on its own

recall.model: Shared keywords miss the point: a ticket that says money back shares no word with one that says refund. I'd turn every past ticket into an embedding with an embedding model, once, and embed each new ticket with the same model, so tickets that mean the same thing get nearby vectors. The tool then shows the nearest few past tickets by cosine similarity. Before trusting any cut-off, I'd collect pairs the team has already marked as same or different, score them, and count the mistakes on both sides of the line, then choose the line from that. And similar isn't the same: the tool should put matches in front of a person to confirm, not merge or close tickets on its own.

recall.prompt: Bottle 47's card is 2, 1, 3, 0, 1, 1 and bottle 212's is 6, 3, 9, 0, 3, 3. Which is true?
options: Cosine similarity 0.33, because 212's arrow is three times as long
Cosine similarity 1.00 and straight-line distance 8.00: same direction, different lengths
Cosine similarity 1.00 and straight-line distance 0.00: they are the same point
Cosine similarity 0.33 and straight-line distance 8.00: different in every way
recall.why: Every score on 212 is three times 47's, so the arrows point the same way: dot product 48, lengths 4 and 12, cosine 48 / 48 = 1. Their tips are 8 apart, because 212 reaches three times as far. Cosine ignores length; distance doesn't. Only normalizing would put them on the same point.

recall.prompt: A new teammate reads that a provider's embeddings all come at length 1, and that with them dot product, cosine and straight-line distance give the same ranking. Explain why that holds, and what such vectors can no longer tell you.

keyIdeas.idea: Cosine is the dot product divided by both lengths, so when both lengths are 1 the dot product is the cosine
Between vectors of length 1, distance depends only on the angle, so a smaller distance always means a higher cosine
Normalizing throws length away, so whatever length carried, like strength, size or popularity, is gone

recall.model: Cosine similarity is the dot product divided by both vectors' lengths. When every length is 1, that division changes nothing, so the dot product is the cosine, and it's cheaper to compute. Between vectors of length 1, the straight-line distance depends only on the angle: distance squared is 2 minus 2 times the cosine, so the closer two vectors are, the higher their cosine, and the two rankings come out in the same order. What's gone is length. If two things differed mainly in strength, size or how often they were seen, normalized vectors can't show it, the way Honorine's cologne and its extrait become the same point.

recall.prompt: Ranked by straight-line distance, 47 finds Linen Water first, a faint scent for sheets, though cosine ranks it third and puts 212 first. Why?
options: Distance can only compare scents that share their strongest note
Linen Water's card was scored by a different hand, so it sits closer
Short arrows sit near every other short arrow, so length decides much of the distance
Distance and cosine always rank alike, so the gap is a rounding error
recall.why: Linen Water has length 1.73 and 47 has length 4, so their tips are only 2.65 apart, though the arrows point 30 degrees apart. 212 points exactly the same way as 47 but reaches three times as far, so its tip is 8.00 away. Distance mixes strength into the score; cosine leaves it out.

recall.prompt: A provider's embedding model returns 1,536 numbers for each piece of text. What does the 412th number mean?
options: How strongly the text is about one topic, as listed in the provider's documentation
The token id of the 412th token in the text
How similar the text is to the 412th document stored so far
Usually nothing a person can name: meaning lives in where the whole vector sits
recall.why: Learned dimensions rarely have names: Google's course says the individual dimensions are rarely as understandable as dessertness or liquidness. What carries meaning is the whole vector's position among the others, its angle and distance to them. Honorine's six named notes are a teaching simplification.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 5 months later. The archive's website has been live since March, with a smells-like-this panel on every bottle's page. Lucien hired a contractor, Arvid, to make it smarter. Honorine's cards are not used any more: the vectors are now learned from visitors, so bottles people view in the same visit end up near each other. To keep pages quick, Arvid ranks the panel by plain dot product on those raw vectors. Since then, almost every page suggests the same four bottles, the four most viewed, even pages for scents nothing like them. Blue Hour's page now suggests Chapel Smoke. I printed the vectors: those four have the biggest numbers in the archive, three or four times the others in every position.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why do the same four bottles turn up on every page, and what would you change?

keyIdeas.idea: A raw dot product grows with both vectors' lengths, so the four with the longest vectors win almost everywhere
Popular bottles were seen in so many visits that their vectors grew long: the panel now measures popularity, not scent
Rank by cosine, or normalize every vector to length 1 before the dot product, so only direction counts
Decide on purpose how much popularity may count, then check the panel on real pages, including scents nobody views

coldCase.model: The dot product multiplies two vectors number by number and adds the results, so it grows with their lengths as well as with how closely they point the same way. The four most viewed bottles were seen in so many visits that their vectors grew long, three or four times the rest, and a long vector wins a raw dot product on almost any page. Google's recommendation course describes exactly this: frequently seen items tend to get large norms and can dominate. The panel now measures popularity, not scent. I'd rank by cosine, or normalize every vector to length 1 before the dot product, so only direction counts. If Lucien wants popular bottles to get a small boost, add it on purpose as a separate, visible part of the score. Then I'd check the panel on a sample of real pages, including scents nobody views, before and after the change.

sources.title: Mikolov, Chen, Corrado and Dean (Google), Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space, arXiv 1301.3781, 2013: two architectures for continuous vector representations of words from very large data sets (continuous bag-of-words and skip-gram); words as atomic units with no notion of similarity, represented as indices in a vocabulary; similar words tend to be close to each other, with multiple degrees of similarity; 8,869 semantic and 10,675 syntactic test questions; biggest minus big plus small, answered by the closest word measured by cosine; high quality word vectors from a 1.6 billion word data set in less than a day

Mikolov, Yih and Zweig (Microsoft Research), Linguistic Regularities in Continuous Space Word Representations, NAACL-HLT 2013, pages 746 to 751: relation-specific vector offsets; King minus Man plus Woman results in a vector very close to Queen; vectors normalized to unit norm and the answer is the word with the greatest cosine similarity, since no word might exist at that exact position; almost 40 percent of the syntactic analogy questions answered correctly

OpenAI, Vector embeddings guide: embeddings measure the relatedness of text strings; an embedding is a vector (list) of floating point numbers; small distances suggest high relatedness; default lengths 1536 (text-embedding-3-small) and 3072 (text-embedding-3-large); billed by input tokens; FAQ: we recommend cosine similarity, the choice typically doesn't matter much, embeddings are normalized to length 1, so cosine can be computed slightly faster with a dot product and cosine and Euclidean distance give identical rankings; uses include search and recommendations

Anthropic, Embeddings (Claude Platform docs): Anthropic does not offer its own embedding model and points to Voyage AI; voyage-4 returns vectors of 1024 numbers; quickstart nearest-neighbour search by dot product with the same model for documents and query; Voyage AI embeddings are normalized to length 1, so dot-product and cosine similarity are the same and cosine and Euclidean distance give identical rankings

Google Machine Learning Crash Course, Embeddings: embedding space and static embeddings: distance between items as a measure of relative similarity; the individual dimensions are rarely as understandable as dessertness or liquidness; for word embeddings d is often 256, 512 or 1024; word2vec, an older example largely superseded by other models, gives a single global embedding per word (a static embedding); static embeddings represent all meanings of a word with a single point

Google, Recommendation Systems course, Candidate generation: similarity measures (cosine, dot product, Euclidean distance); Items A, B and C ranked differently by each measure; if the embeddings are normalized, dot product and cosine coincide and squared Euclidean distance coincides up to a constant; the dot product is sensitive to the norm; items that appear very frequently in the training set tend to have large norms, and popular items may end up dominating the recommendations
